children: By Jacob Passy
Airbnb, long attacked for worsening housing affordability in major cities, is now looking to tackle the problem.

The short-term rental company is committing an initial $250 million investment toward housing projects. The money will serve as gap financing for developments with a funding shortfall, with priority given to affordable and mixed-income housing projects. The first chunk is going toward a roughly 200-unit affordable-housing development in Austin, Texas.
"We've been embroiled in lots of debates with cities about whether or not Airbnb is a contributor to housing becoming unaffordable," Airbnb Chief Executive Brian Chesky said in an interview.

Under the Airbnb Housing Accelerator program, the company will distribute the $250 million to developers to help them bridge gaps in financing multifamily housing projects. Airbnb will solicit applications from developers through the housing accelerator's website. The company said its returns will be below market rates.
The program will primarily focus on the U.S., but the company hasn't ruled out expanding it to other markets where it operates.

While the $250 million investment won't solve the housing affordability crisis alone, industry veterans say it will help spur additional investments and lead to more housing being built. Airbnb plans to reinvest the funds it recoups into additional projects.

Housing affordability has become a powerful political issue, locally and nationally, as costs have soared. Airbnb, which reported $2.5 billion in net income on $12.2 billion in revenue last year, and the broader business for short-term rentals have become targets. Critics say these rentals have contributed to housing shortages by tying up homes and apartments that might otherwise be people's full-time residences. Some cities have heavily restricted such rentals.
Units rented via Airbnb are a tiny fraction of housing, and bans on Airbnb in cities haven't resulted in home prices falling, Chesky said.

"I've just lived in the crosshairs of the number one political issue in most major cities in America. And I can't stare at the problem for much longer without Airbnb trying to offer up some solutions," he said. "I think it can benefit Airbnb, but I think this is primarily not about Airbnb."

Airbnb selected the project in Austin in part because of efforts undertaken by city and state lawmakers to revise regulations to promote home construction, said Daniel Hornung, a former Biden administration official who was tapped to serve as the Housing Accelerator initiative's director.
"We want to make sure that our investments are catalytic and are demonstrating proof of concept about new models that can work," he said.

In Austin, Airbnb will be providing $6.4 million in financing. The project will be on the former site of a Home Depot and a car dealership in the city's St. John neighborhood, which is a majority-minority area. The city purchased the 20-acre tract of land over 10 years ago and originally planned to build government facilities there. Since then, the site has sat empty and become an eyesore, said Chito Vela, an Austin city council member whose district includes the project.
"Things were moving along pretty well until we started to see interest rates go up and started to see rents go down in Austin," Vela said. "All of a sudden the financing got really wobbly."

Airbnb's funding will go toward around 200 affordable housing units as part of the broader planned complex at the St. John site. Residents of the affordable-housing units won't be allowed to list their units for short-term rental.

"This is Airbnb asking the question of how it can use its balance sheet and the resources available to it to contribute to improving housing affordability," Hornung said. "The goal of this is not at all to create more Airbnb supply."

The run-up in interest rates in recent years has complicated efforts to fund affordable housing projects, said Shaun Donovan, who was housing and urban development secretary during the Obama administration.

"You're not going to be able to charge more for the rents because it's affordable housing," Donovan said. "So every time the interest rates go up, it subtracts the amount of market-rate capital you're able to attract for the deal, and it creates gaps that you have to go fill somewhere else."

Estimates as to the scale of the country's housing shortage vary widely, said Donovan, who is now the chief executive of national housing nonprofit Enterprise Community Partners. Some suggest the U.S. is missing around two million housing units, while others peg the figure at around 10 million.

Donovan said the type of funding Airbnb is providing can have an outsize impact by unlocking significantly more funding for housing projects, but addressing the housing shortfall nationwide will take tens of billions of dollars. "You're not going to solve this crisis with money alone," he said.

The $250 million that Airbnb is distributing will "get those deals over the finish line," Hornung said. He said the individual investments Airbnb makes will generally represent about 10% of the capital for each of the projects in question.
Over a decade, Airbnb expects the initial $250 million investment will translate into $5 billion of capital, Hornung said.

Airbnb's housing initiative also will support advocacy efforts aimed at changing regulations around zoning, permitting and building codes. The accelerator will further create an open-source data set tracking housing policies and launch a competition to award $5 million to companies or nonprofits developing technology to simplify building homes.
